_comment: Phase 8 retrieval-quality golden set (docs/DECISIONS.md D8.1). A purpose-built corpus, not scripts/seed.mjs's 3 demo documents (too thin for meaningful hit@K/MRR — see that entry). Each document is real prose about this app's own architecture so overlap between documents is realistic (several mention embeddings, indexing, or retrieval), which is what makes hit@K/MRR meaningful instead of trivial. relevantTitles is the document-level ground truth scripts/eval-retrieval.mjs checks each returned chunk's document_title against.

documents.title: Chunking Strategy
documents.content:
# Chunking Strategy

Before a document can be searched, it has to be split into chunks small enough to embed meaningfully and large enough to carry real context. The chunker in packages/rag-core walks a document's Markdown structure and packs text toward a soft token budget — 450 tokens by default — never letting a single chunk's own content cross a hard ceiling of 600 tokens.

Each chunk after the first carries roughly 60 tokens of trailing context copied from the end of the previous chunk. This overlap means a sentence that happens to fall right on a chunk boundary still has a reasonable chance of showing up, with its surrounding context, in at least one retrieved chunk — losing a sentence entirely to an unlucky boundary would otherwise make an answer look like it ignored part of the document.

A trailing chunk that ends up under about 80 tokens gets merged into the chunk before it rather than left to stand alone, since a tiny fragment chunk rarely carries enough context to be useful on its own and just adds noise to retrieval. Headings are tracked as the chunker walks the document, so every chunk also carries a heading path — the chain of section headings above it, starting with the document's own title — which both the embedding step and the citation UI make use of.

Token counts come from the real BPE tokenizer (gpt-tokenizer), not a word or character estimate, so the budget lines up with what the embedding and chat models actually see. Tuning the three knobs — target tokens, max tokens, and overlap tokens — is exactly what the retrieval-quality eval harness sweeps, since chunk size is one of the biggest levers on retrieval quality for a hybrid semantic/keyword system like this one.

documents.title: Embeddings and Vector Search
documents.content:
# Embeddings and Vector Search

Every chunk is turned into a fixed-length numeric vector by an embedding model before it's written to the database, and every chat question is embedded the same way at query time. Two pieces of text whose vectors point in a similar direction are treated as similar in meaning, even if they don't share many exact words — this is what lets the app answer a question phrased very differently from the document's own wording.

Vectors are stored in a pgvector column, sized to exactly 1536 dimensions to match the embedding model's own output width; changing embedding models to one with a different width requires an explicit migration on that column. Similarity between a query vector and a stored chunk vector is computed with cosine distance via pgvector's `<=>` operator, and an HNSW index over the column keeps that search fast even as the number of chunks grows, without ever needing to compare a query against every row in the table.

The app never hard-codes a single embedding provider. A small provider-agnostic layer (`@kb/ai`) exposes one `EmbeddingModel` interface with an `embed()` method, and the concrete implementation behind it — OpenAI, Groq, a local Ollama model, or a keyless deterministic mock used for demos and tests — is chosen entirely from environment variables at startup. The mock model is a dependency-free feature-hashed bag-of-words embedder: deterministic, and texts sharing vocabulary score more similar than unrelated ones, which is exactly what a demo or an automated eval needs without spending any real API budget.

documents.title: Hybrid Retrieval and RRF
documents.content:
# Hybrid Retrieval and RRF

Answering a chat question starts with retrieval, and retrieval here is deliberately hybrid rather than semantic-only. A single Postgres RPC, `match_document_chunks`, runs two independent searches in parallel: a semantic search over chunk embeddings using pgvector's cosine distance, and a keyword search over each chunk's full-text search column using Postgres's own `ts_rank_cd`.

Semantic search is excellent at matching meaning across different wording, but it can miss an exact identifier, error code, or rare proper noun that a keyword search catches instantly — and the reverse is true too, since keyword search is blind to synonyms and paraphrase. Running both and combining the results gets the strengths of each without picking one at the expense of the other.

The two ranked lists are fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF): each chunk's score is the sum of `1 / (60 + rank)` across whichever of the two lists it appears in, using each list's own rank rather than its raw similarity or text-rank score. RRF is deliberately scale-free this way — it never has to reconcile a cosine similarity (roughly 0 to 1) with a `ts_rank_cd` score (an unbounded, corpus-dependent number) on the same axis, which is exactly the kind of ad-hoc weighting that tends to be fragile in practice. The fused, re-ranked list is what chat.service.ts turns into numbered citations in the final answer.

documents.title: Row-Level Security and Auth
documents.content:
# Row-Level Security and Auth

Every table a user's data lives in — documents, document_chunks, ai_usage_events — has Postgres Row-Level Security turned on, and every policy on those tables compares a row's `user_id` column against `auth.uid()`, the id embedded in the caller's own JWT. There is no service-role client anywhere in apps/api; every single request, including background indexing jobs, runs against the database as the actual signed-in user, so the database itself is the enforcement boundary, not application code that could have a bug in it.

Sign-in issues a JWT via Supabase Auth. In local development without Docker, apps/api's AuthGuard has a fallback path that verifies a JWT's HS256 signature directly against a well-known local secret, since a bare `supabase start` has no real GoTrue service to verify against — but that fallback is hard-gated behind `NODE_ENV !== "production"`, so it can never be reached in a real deployment even if the same environment variable were somehow set there. A hosted Supabase project instead verifies through Supabase's own `getClaims()`/JWKS, which uses real asymmetric keys.

RLS isolation is tested directly with pgTAP: `rls_isolation.test.sql` creates two separate users, inserts data as each, and asserts that user B's queries return zero rows of user A's documents and chunks — even when B tries to guess A's document ids outright, not just when browsing normally.

documents.title: Rate Limiting
documents.content:
# Rate Limiting

apps/api throttles requests per user using NestJS's built-in Throttler module, configured with two separate buckets rather than one blanket limit. The default bucket applies to ordinary CRUD routes — creating, listing, editing, and deleting documents — with a generous limit (120 requests per 60 seconds by default) since normal document editing can involve a burst of small requests.

A second, stricter bucket applies only to the chat-streaming endpoint, `POST /chat/stream` — 20 requests per 60 seconds by default — because each chat request triggers at least one real embedding call and one real chat-completion call to whatever AI provider is configured, and those cost real money and real latency in a way a document save doesn't. Both limits are environment-configurable (`THROTTLE_DEFAULT_LIMIT`/`THROTTLE_DEFAULT_TTL_MS` and `THROTTLE_CHAT_LIMIT`/`THROTTLE_CHAT_TTL_MS`), so a deployment that expects much heavier or lighter traffic can tune them without a code change.

A request that exceeds its bucket's limit gets a 429 response rather than being queued or silently dropped, so the client — apps/web's own fetch wrapper — can show the user a clear "you're doing that too fast, try again shortly" message instead of a request that just seems to hang.

documents.title: Citations and Highlighting
documents.content:
# Citations and Highlighting

Every answer the chat endpoint streams back includes numbered citations tied to the exact chunks retrieval returned, not just a generic "based on your documents" disclaimer. Each citation carries the source document's id along with the precise character range — `charStart`/`charEnd` — that chunk covers in that document's current content, computed once during chunking and stored alongside the chunk itself.

Clicking a citation in the chat UI navigates to `/documents/:id?highlight=start-end`. The document editor reads that query param on mount, switches to its Write tab (already the default), and calls the browser's native `textarea.setSelectionRange()` with the clamped start/end offsets — which both scrolls the exact passage into view and highlights it using the browser's own text-selection rendering, with no separate rich-text highlighter needed for what's otherwise a plain textarea.

Because the highlighted range is computed against the chunk's own stored `char_start`/`char_end`, it's only ever valid against the exact content that chunk was produced from — which is the same reason a stale chunk (one left over from before an edit that hasn't finished reindexing yet) must never be retrievable in the first place; see the Content Hash and Stale Chunk Prevention document for how that's enforced.

documents.title: Document Indexing Status
documents.content:
# Document Indexing Status

Saving a document doesn't index it synchronously — indexing is queued and processed in the background so the save request itself stays fast. A document's `index_status` moves through a small state machine: `pending` right after a save, `indexing` once a background job actually picks it up, then either `ready` on success or `failed` on error, with a human-readable `index_error` message set alongside a failure.

The document editor shows this status as a badge next to the title, and a `failed` status renders a one-click Retry button that re-enqueues the same document for indexing. Retrying doesn't touch the document's content at all — it only asks the pipeline to try chunking and embedding the current content again, which is exactly what you want when a failure was caused by something transient like an embedding provider timing out, not by anything wrong with the document itself.

If the API process crashes or restarts while jobs are mid-flight, a startup sweep looks for any document still stuck in `indexing` and re-enqueues it — otherwise it would sit there forever showing "indexing" with no job left running to ever finish it. Every one of these transitions is guarded by the document's current `content_hash`, so a job that was queued for an older version of the document is a safe no-op rather than clobbering a newer edit's own status.

documents.title: Tags and Scoping Retrieval
documents.content:
# Tags and Scoping Retrieval

A chat question doesn't have to search every document a user owns. The chat composer lets a question be scoped three ways: to all documents, to a specific set of document ids (e.g. "ask about this doc" from a document's own page), or to a set of tags.

Tags are a small, free-form string array on each document — up to 20 per document — indexed with a GIN index so filtering by tag stays fast even with a large document set. When a chat request includes a tag filter, `match_document_chunks` applies it as `d.tags && filter_tags` (Postgres's array-overlap operator) at the same query stage as the content-hash freshness check, after the initial ANN/GIN top-K fetch but before the final fused ranking — so a document just needs to share at least one tag with the filter, not match all of them, and tag filtering never has to scan every chunk in the database to do it.

Document-id scoping works the same way, as an explicit `document_id = any(filter_document_ids)` check — and because it's applied inside the same RLS-scoped query as everything else, naming another user's document id in that filter (even by guessing it outright) simply returns zero rows rather than leaking whether that id even exists.

documents.title: Chat Streaming
documents.content:
# Chat Streaming

`POST /chat/stream` returns its answer as Server-Sent Events, not a single JSON response, so the answer appears token by token as the model generates it rather than all at once after a long wait. The client-side hook driving this, `use-chat-stream.ts`, moves through explicit phases as the response arrives — sending, searching (retrieval is running), streaming (tokens are arriving), and settled (the assistant message's final row has actually landed in history) — and the UI reads that phase to decide what to show, rather than inferring state from timing.

That last phase matters more than it might look: a message can start streaming into view well before its corresponding database row exists, so anything that decides "is the assistant done replying" purely by matching a message id, without also checking that its status has actually settled to something terminal, can treat an in-progress reply as finished. That exact bug — and the fix, checking status alongside id — is documented in docs/DECISIONS.md's Phase 6 chat/UX audit.

The stream is abortable: navigating away or unmounting the chat view cancels the in-flight request via `AbortController` rather than letting a response the user can no longer see keep consuming tokens and provider quota in the background.

documents.title: Usage and Cost Tracking
documents.content:
# Usage and Cost Tracking

Every real call to an AI provider — embedding a chunk during indexing, embedding a chat query, generating a chat completion, or rewriting a query for retrieval — records a row in `ai_usage_events`: the operation type, the provider and model, prompt/completion/total token counts, whether those counts were reported by the provider or estimated locally, and latency.

The Usage page in apps/web reads that table and rolls it up by day, by operation, and by model, so it's possible to see at a glance whether a spike in cost came from a burst of chat questions, from re-indexing a lot of documents at once, or from a single unusually expensive model. Estimated-token rows (from a provider that doesn't report usage in its streaming response) are flagged as such rather than silently presented as exact, since an estimate and a provider-reported count aren't the same kind of number.

Recording usage is deliberately best-effort and happens strictly after the real provider call it's describing: if the usage insert itself fails for some reason, that failure is logged and swallowed rather than allowed to turn an otherwise-successful embedding or chat call into a reported error, since the tokens were already spent by the time accounting runs.

documents.title: Markdown Editing
documents.content:
# Markdown Editing

Documents are written and edited as plain Markdown in a textarea, with a Preview tab rendering the same content through `react-markdown` so what a reader will eventually see in a citation or export is easy to check without leaving the editor. Saving is available both as an explicit Save button and as the familiar Cmd/Ctrl+S shortcut, and a native `beforeunload` handler warns before closing a tab or typing a new URL while there are unsaved changes.

Background activity can update a document out from under an editor that's open in a browser tab — most commonly a background poll picking up a finished index. The form only ever adopts that fresh server data into fields the user hasn't touched since the request that produced it was sent: a field whose live value still exactly matches what was last sent to the server adopts the server's version, while a field the user has since changed keeps the user's edit, and is correctly flagged as unsaved against the new baseline. Overwriting the whole draft unconditionally on any server response used to silently discard keystrokes typed during a save or a reindex retry — the sort of bug that's easy to miss in casual testing because it only shows up when typing happens to overlap a request that's still in flight.

The retry-indexing button reads the document's currently-typed content at the moment it's clicked, not at the moment its request resolves, for the same reason: a plain closure over `dirty` state can go stale across an `await`.

documents.title: Content Hash and Stale Chunk Prevention
documents.content:
# Content Hash and Stale Chunk Prevention

Every document has a `content_hash` — a SHA-256 digest of its title and content — that changes exactly when either of those changes. Saving a document with new content computes a new hash immediately; the chunks and embeddings that match the OLD hash aren't valid for the new content anymore, since chunking and embedding are what actually produce the text retrieval searches over.

Each chunk written by the indexing pipeline is stamped with the `content_hash` of the document it was chunked FROM, at write time. `match_document_chunks` only ever returns a chunk whose stored `content_hash` still equals its document's CURRENT `content_hash` — applied at the same query stage as the tag filter, right after the initial ANN/GIN top-K fetch, so the check stays index-friendly instead of forcing a full scan.

Without this check, a document mid-reindex (or one whose last reindex attempt failed outright) would keep serving up its previous, now-stale chunks as if they were still accurate — and because a chunk's citation range is only valid against the exact content it was chunked from, an answer built from a stale chunk could highlight the wrong span entirely, or one that no longer says what the citation implies it says. `replace_document_chunks` enforces the same freshness rule from the write side: it silently declines to write chunks for a content_hash the document has already moved past, rather than ever risking two different reindex attempts racing to overwrite the same document's chunks out of order.
